title: Coaching for adaptive expertise
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes reviews a new paper by Walsh, Matsumura, Schunn and Zook-Howell on Mental Simulations for Teacher Reflection (MSTR) and treats it as the missing operational manual for instructional coaching. Her framing problem is the knowing-doing gap: professional development supplies frameworks, but under real classroom unpredictability teachers revert to familiar routines, because adaptive teaching requires pedagogical reasoning rather than technique recall. MSTR is described as a structured post-lesson routine, usually video-based, in which coach and teacher surface ambiguity, generate multiple plausible alternative moves, weigh tradeoffs, and connect choices back to learning goals. The paper's empirical hook, which Hughes leans on, is that coaches whose teachers went on to show substantial instructional growth were markedly more likely to run genuine mental-simulation talk rather than evaluative surface feedback. She converts this into five coaching prescriptions - treat MSTR as a phased routine, surface ambiguity even when the lesson went fine, insist on multiple alternatives rather than one fix, tie every option to student thinking, and document and revisit the decisions. She is candid about the limits: MSTR depends on skilled facilitation, psychological safety, authentic artefacts, and repeated cycles, and without those it collapses back into superficial feedback. She also notes she is running mental simulation as the golden thread of whole-school PD in the school where she currently leads development.
points: Hughes's central claim is that 'reflection' has been left undefined in PD design, and MSTR's contribution is naming the sub-components of a good coaching conversation so they can be trained rather than left to individual style.

The discriminating evidence is behavioural: high-growth coaches initiated the routine themselves instead of waiting for the teacher to confess a problem, and generated a range of alternatives from minor tweaks to major redesigns.
The most counter-intuitive coaching instruction is to surface ambiguity when a lesson went okay, since the lessons that produce no obvious error are the ones where reasoning is never rehearsed.
She insists alternatives be tied to conceptual learning goals rather than behaviour or compliance, which is her dividing line between pedagogical reasoning and classroom management talk.

The limitations section is load-bearing: without authentic artefacts, time, psychological safety and repeated cycles, mental simulation becomes hypothetical and coaching reverts to evaluative feedback.
quotes: There is growing consensus in education that high-quality teaching doesn’t just require well-designed lesson plans, it demands adaptive expertise; teachers must be able to respond in real time to unpredictable classroom dynamics, notice student thinking, make pedagogical decisions on the fly and adjust their teaching moves accordingly. But while many professional development programs claim to aim for that, few give coaches concrete, replicable tools for building adaptive expertise.

One persistent problem in teacher development is the so-called ‘knowing–doing gap.’ Many PD programs give teachers relevant pedagogical frameworks; yet when it comes to real classroom practice, with its unpredictability, diverse learners, unexpected responses, teachers often revert to familiar routines.

Because adaptive teaching isn’t just about knowing techniques. It’s about developing deep pedagogical reasoning: noticing what’s happening with student thinking, interpreting that in light of learning goals, generating multiple possible responses and choosing flexibly.

Unfortunately, many professional learning designs remain vague about how to cultivate that kind of reasoning. Coaches may review videos or student work with teachers, but without structured scaffolding, such reflection sessions can drift toward surface-level feedback eg., “Next time ask more open questions” rather than deep reasoning about student thinking.

Crucially, the paper doesn’t just name these phases: it identifies finer-grain subcomponents and shows through a detailed illustrative vignette how a strong MSTR conversation unfolds in real life. In effect, MSTR transforms reflection from a vague after-thought into a disciplined, hypothesis-driven, decision-making rehearsal - a kind of ‘mental laboratory’ for teaching.

As the authors themselves note, while MSTR shows great promise, it also depends on skilled facilitation. Not all coaches will naturally lead productive mental simulations: it requires comfort with ambiguity, ability to scaffold reasoning, and fluency in pedagogical concepts. Without that, conversations may revert to superficial feedback.

Teaching is not like other routine jobs: it thrives on uncertainty, relationships, student thinking, conditions that rarely fit tidy scripts or one-size-fits-all routines. If we want teachers who can respond flexibly, thoughtfully, and principledly to real classrooms - adaptive experts - then we need professional learning that reflects that complexity.
